The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. The dataset spans 21 days of normal operation and 6 days of controlled attack execution, comprising approximately 310 million packets. Eight attack scenarios were implemented: function code scanning, coil mass-write injection, replay with modified values, man-in-the-middle payload substitution, time-synchronisation offset injection, denial-of-service flooding, slow-rate polling exhaustion, and firmware update spoofing. UA supports three security modes—None, Sign, and SignAndEncrypt—and this paper evaluates how each mode affects the discriminability of traffic features used in unsupervised anomaly detectors. Experiments were conducted on a testbed comprising an OPC UA server, two client applications, and an embedded data historian. Seventeen traffic features extractable from unencrypted traffic were assessed for their availability under Sign and SignAndEncrypt modes using packet capture before and after the application layer. Under SignAndEncrypt, 11 of 17 features became unavailable or uninformative at the packet level; however, timing, packet length distribution, and session-level handshake frequency remained discriminative. The dataset spans 21 days of normal operation and 6 days of controlled attack execution, comprising approximately 310 million packets. Eight attack scenarios were implemented: function code scanning, coil mass-write injection, replay with modified values, man-in-the-middle payload substitution, time-synchronisation offset injection, denial-of-service flooding, slow-rate polling exhaustion, and firmware update spoofing. Each packet is labelled with a binary normal/attack flag and a scenario identifier.
